newsitem.title: USA: Dollar higher after U.S. trade gap shrinks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar higher after U.S. trade gap shrinks.

text.p: The dollar rose on Thursday, helped by a surprise drop in the United States international trade deficit, which hinted the strong U.S. currency may not be damaging U.S. exports.

A jump in U.S. aircraft exports contributed largely to the 30.2 percent contraction in the October trade deficit in goods and services on Thursday. The overall trade gap narrowed to $7.99 billion from $11.44 billion in September.

Traders often purchase dollars when the deficit shrinks because it reduces the risk the government will try to weaken the currency to make exports cheaper abroad. In this case, the market got a much smaller gap than it expected.

"The only reason why the dollar went up is because of the trade number," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank in New York. "If it was anything less than $9 billion down they were going to buy dollars, which they did."
But aircraft orders can rise and fall sharply on a month- to-month basis and not all aspects of the trade data were considered good news for the dollar.

Although the dollar rushed above 1.56 marks and rose to a two-year high against the Swiss franc after the number, it gave back some of its gains. Against the yen it made little headway after the data, because the bilateral trade gap with Japan widened.
The dollar ended at 1.5575 marks on Thursday, up from 1.5517 on Wednesday. It rose to 114.03 yen from 113.69 yen.
The 31-percent jump in the deficit with Japan mirrored Japanese trade data on Wednesday, which showed a surge in Japanese auto exports to the U.S. due to the cheaper yen against the dollar this year.

"The trade numbers overall here are better. But with Japan they are not going to get any better with this dollar the way it is," said John Barlow, senior foreign exchange dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale.

The trade data compares how much the U.S. earns from sales overseas to its payments for foreign merchandise and services such as banking and insurance. A declining deficit nets more revenues from exports and boosts economic growth forecasts.

Traders also said the dollar garnered psychological support from Wall Street, where stock and bond prices stormed higher on Thursday. Bonds usually decline when signs of a strong economy push interest rates higher.

"The reason for the move up, basically, is that the trade figures showed the economy is moving pretty good," Barlow said. "Yet the asset markets are holding on so I think that is like a double-bonus effect."
Elsewhere, the dollar ended at 1.3395 Swiss francs, up from 1.3295 on Wednesday. It rose to Canadian $1.3670 from C$1.3667. The pound fell to $1.6647 from $1.6747.
